title: Coexistence of Magnon-Induced Optical Vortex and Gaussian Beam Scattering Assisted by Rotational Umklapp Process
authors: Ryusuke Hisatomi, Kotaro Taga, Hisakazu Matsuki, Shutaro Karube, Yoichi Shiota, Teruo Ono
abstract: The exploitation of crystal-lattice symmetries to engineer angular momentum transfer between structured light and magnons marks a novel frontier for optomagnonic research. In Brillouin light scattering, when focused light propagates parallel to an external magnetic field and interacts with ferromagnetic uniform magnons, only optical-vortex scattering is expected to be permitted. Due to the combined effects of magneto-optical coupling and optical spin-orbit interaction, the transfer of magnon spin angular momentum to photon orbital angular momentum allows for this distinctive scattering phenomenon. Here, we experimentally demonstrate that, for a specific ferromagnetic crystal orientation, Gaussian-beam scattering coexists with the optical-vortex scattering, contrary to conventional expectations based on angular momentum conservation between magnons and photons. We show that the crystal lattice, via the rotational Umklapp process, provides the missing angular momentum required for the Gaussian-beam scattering. Furthermore, we predict that as the degree of light focusing increases, the relative efficiencies of the Gaussian-beam and optical-vortex scattering processes reverse.
summary: This research explores magnon-induced Brillouin light scattering in YIG crystals, demonstrating the coexistence of two scattering types: vortex and Gaussian-beam. The key finding is that the crystal lattice's rotational Umklapp process enables the Gaussian-beam scattering, which contradicts simple angular momentum conservation rules. The relative strength of these two processes is shown to be highly dependent on how tightly the light is focused.
main_problem: The paper investigates the coexistence of two distinct magnon-induced Brillouin light scattering (BLS) pathways: optical-vortex scattering and Gaussian-beam scattering, challenging conventional angular momentum conservation rules.
main_result: The coexistence is experimentally demonstrated and theoretically explained by invoking the rotational Umklapp process provided by the crystal lattice, leading to a predicted reversal in the relative efficiencies of the two scattering channels with increasing light focusing.
method: The study combines experimental measurements of scattering efficiencies using optical heterodyne detection with theoretical calculations based on a microscopic framework involving spin-orbit-coupled light modes.
model_or_system: The experiment uses a spherical YIG single crystal oriented along the <111> axis, studying the interaction between focused light and uniform magnons (Kittel mode) under an external magnetic field.
key_observables: Scattering efficiencies ($\eta$) for Stokes and anti-Stokes sidebands, measured for both helicity-inversion (Gaussian-beam) and helicity-conserving (optical-vortex) processes.
important_parameters: External magnetic field orientation ($\mathbf{H} \parallel \langle 111 angle$), light focusing degree (related to NA), and the magnon resonance frequency ($\omega_m/2\pi = 4.10$ GHz).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the crystal lattice mediates the necessary angular momentum via the rotational Umklapp process, and that the light can be modeled as converting from paraxial to spin-orbit-coupled modes under strong focusing.
figures_summary: Figure 1 details the experimental setup and confirms the magnon resonance. Figure 2 presents measured BLS efficiencies comparing Gaussian-beam and optical-vortex scattering. Figure 3 illustrates the dependence of scattering efficiencies on the degree of light focusing (NA).
paper_structure: The paper establishes the theoretical background in optomagnonics, details the experimental setup and measurements of two scattering channels, provides theoretical derivations for the scattering efficiencies using a microscopic framework, and concludes by analyzing the dependence of the relative efficiencies on light focusing.
why_interesting: This work bridges quantum optics (structured light, OAM/SAM) with condensed matter magnetism (magnons) by identifying a symmetry-breaking mechanism (Umklapp process) that allows for novel light-matter interactions, relevant to engineered quantum light sources.
